analysis.one_liner: Lets truck drivers drive longer hours and lets 18-year-olds get commercial driver's licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had zero cosponsors, never left the Senate Commerce Committee and died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the Transportation Department to rewrite truck safety rules so property-carrying truck drivers can drive up to 12 hours a day instead of 11, with a 14-hour on-duty window, more rest-break options, and a carve-out letting drivers finish a trip past those limits if they are within 150 miles of the destination. It would also lower the minimum age for a commercial driver's license from 21 to 18. Separately, it requires reports from the Transportation Department and a study by the Government Accountability Office on the costs and effectiveness of electronic logging devices, the devices that record driving time.
analysis.who_benefits: Trucking companies and freight shippers gain the most: more driving hours per driver per day means more freight moved with fewer drivers, and an 18-year-old hiring pool lowers labor costs. Some drivers would get scheduling flexibility, including a choice of shorter driving stretches with built-in breaks and exclusion of certain time from the on-duty clock.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the maximum driving time for property-carrying truck drivers from 11 hours to 12 hours within a 24-hour period [S3].
It gives drivers an elective schedule of 8 hours of driving with two to four 30-minute rest breaks, and counts rest breaks as off-duty time excluded from the 14-hour on-duty clock [S3].
A driver within 150 miles of the trip's stated destination may keep driving past the 12-hour driving limit and 14-hour on-duty limit until reaching that destination [S3].
It lowers the minimum age for obtaining a commercial driver's license from 21 to 18 [S2].

It requires the Transportation Department to report on how it reviews electronic logging device logs and how operators can appeal violations, and requires a Government Accountability Office study on the costs and effectiveness of those devices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who shares the road with trucks bears a higher risk of fatigue-related crashes, since longer maximum driving shifts and drivers as young as 18 are both linked to higher crash risk. Drivers themselves face longer shifts behind the wheel and downward wage pressure from a larger, younger labor pool; the bill blocks the Transportation Department from shortening the 14-hour on-duty window or shrinking the 150-mile short-haul radius if it revises those rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Road users and long-haul truck drivers

drawbacks.text: Longer maximum driving shifts increase the risk of fatigue-related truck crashes; hours-of-service limits exist specifically to cap how long a driver can stay behind the wheel [S3].
Lowering the commercial licensing age to 18 puts 18-, 19-, and 20-year-olds behind the wheel of 80,000-pound vehicles in interstate commerce; 21 was the long-standing federal minimum [S2].
The 150-mile 'finish the trip' carve-out lets a driver keep driving after hitting the daily limits, so the stated maximum hours are not actually the maximum [S3].

The reporting and study provisions produce no rule change; they only require the Transportation Department and the Government Accountability Office to write reports on electronic logging devices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is pitched as driver flexibility, and the elective shorter-schedule option with mandated breaks is genuinely more flexible than current law. But its headline effects run the other way: longer maximum driving shifts, a loophole that erases the limits near the end of a trip, and a younger licensing age all expand hours and labor supply in ways that chiefly benefit carriers and shippers, while the crash-risk cost falls on drivers and everyone else on the road. The safety-reporting provisions add paperwork but no new protections.

outcome.mechanism: Mike Lee introduced it with no cosponsors, the Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill on October 21, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Truck drivers and everyone else on the road, since the existing hours-of-service limits and the 21-year-old licensing age stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Truck drivers and the motoring public

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only congressional action: read twice and referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up: no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on from either party, so the partisan shape of support never formed.

industries.note: Longer daily driving hours, a finish-the-trip loophole, and an 18-year-old hiring pool would let carriers move more freight with fewer and cheaper drivers. The cost — higher fatigue-crash risk and wage pressure — falls on drivers and the public, not on carriers.

Drivers gain elective schedules with built-in breaks and some time excluded from the on-duty clock, and younger people gain a path into the trade. But longer maximum shifts and a larger labor pool tend to increase fatigue and hold wages down.

industries.industry: Electronic logging device makers and fleet compliance firms
industries.note: The bill orders reviews of how the government audits driver logs and a study of the devices' costs and effectiveness, with appeal rights for operators cited for violations. It imposes no new rules, but frames the devices' costs for scrutiny rather than affirming their safety purpose.
